claim: Subcortical brain structures such as the subthalamic nucleus or the thalamus are involved in regulating motor and cognitive behavior.
source: Subcortical brain structures such as the subthalamic nucleus or the thalamus are involved in regulating motor and cognitive behavior.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data from this study.

claim: The contribution of subcortical structures to perceptual consciousness remains unclear due to the inherent difficulties of recording subcortical neuronal activity in humans.
source: However, their contribution to perceptual consciousness remains unclear, due to the inherent difficulties of recording subcortical neuronal activity in humans.
evidence: This is presented as a gap in current knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: 50 putative single neurons were isolated from the subthalamic nucleus and thalamus during the study.
source: We isolated 50 putative single neurons (STN: 26, Thal: 24) according to spike sorting metrics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–G).
evidence: This is directly reported data from the experimental recordings.

claim: A significant proportion of neurons modulated their activity while participants were expecting a stimulus.
source: A significant proportion of neurons modulated their activity while participants were expecting a stimulus.
evidence: This is a summary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in the results section.

claim: 23% of neurons that modulated during stimulus expectation showed different firing rates between detected and undetected stimuli.
source: We found that the firing rate of 23% of these neurons differed between detected and undetected stimuli.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: The results provide direct neurophysiological evidence of the involvement of the subthalamic nucleus and the thalamus for the detection of vibrotactile stimuli.
source: Our results provide direct neurophysiological evidence of the involvement of the subthalamic nucleus and the thalamus for the detection of vibrotactile stimuli, thereby calling for a less cortico-centric view of the neural correlates of consciousness.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Current methods to investigate neural correlates of consciousness contrast neural activity associated with different percepts under constant sensory stimulation.
source: Current methods to investigate the neural correlates of consciousness aim at contrasting the neural activity associated with different percepts under constant sensory stimulation to identify the minimal set of neuronal events sufficient for a specific conscious percept to occur (Koch et al., 2016; Seth and Bayne, 2022).
evidence: This is established methodology cited from the literature.

claim: Researchers have documented neural correlates of detection in rodents, birds, and nonhuman primates using invasive electrophysiology.
source: Taking advantage of the wealth of invasive electrophysiology recordings available, researchers have documented such correlates with detection tasks in rodents (Schmack et al., 2021), birds (Nieder et al., 2020), and nonhuman primates (de Lafuente and Romo, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in animal models.

claim: The use of animal models to study consciousness raises specific ethical concerns.
source: However, the use of animal models to study consciousness raises specific ethical concerns (Mazor et al., 2023) and requires interpreting behavioral responses with caution (Birch et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature discussing ethical issues.

claim: Only very few studies have found neural correlates of consciousness at the single neuron level in humans, and only in cortical regions.
source: Indeed, only very few studies have found such correlates at the single neuron level (Fried et al., 1997; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2021; Quiroga et al., 2008; Reber et al., 2017) and only in cortical regions.
evidence: This is a summary of the state of the literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: The role of subcortical structures for perceptual consciousness is theoretically relevant.
source: The role of subcortical structures for perceptual consciousness is theoretically relevant (Aru et al., 2020; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011; Schiff, 2008; Seth and Bayne, 2022; Ward, 2013) with some empirical support from detection studies in nonhuman primates (Haegens et al., 2014; Tauste Campo et al., 2019; Vázquez et al., 2012; Vázquez et al., 2013), as well as functional imaging or local field potentials in humans (Kronemer et al., 2022; Levinson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to theoretical and empirical literature.

claim: It remains unknown how the firing rate of subcortical neurons changes when a stimulus is consciously perceived.
source: Nonetheless, it remains unknown how the firing rate of subcortical neurons changes when a stimulus is consciously perceived.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Single-unit recordings provide higher temporal resolution than functional imaging.
source: Single-unit recordings provide a much higher temporal resolution than functional imaging, which helps assess how the neural correlates of consciousness unfold over time.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the comparative advantages of different recording methods.

claim: Single-unit recordings can expose the variety of functional roles of neurons within subcortical regions.
source: Contrary to local field potentials, single-unit recordings can expose the variety of functional roles of neurons within subcortical regions, thereby offering a potential for a better mechanistic understanding of perceptual consciousness.
evidence: This is a methodological advantage stated based on general knowledge of recording techniques.

claim: Individual neurons were recorded from the subthalamic nucleus and thalamus of human participants during 36 deep brain stimulation surgeries.
source: Here, we recorded individual neurons from the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and thalamus of human participants during 36 deep brain stimulation surgeries.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and sample size.

claim: Participants detected vibrotactile stimuli provided at the perceptual threshold.
source: Participants detected vibrotactile stimuli provided at the perceptual threshold, and we tested how neurons in both subcortical structures were modulated by the task, the onset of the stimulus, or the detection or not of the stimulus.
evidence: This describes the experimental task design.

claim: Microelectrode recordings are performed routinely after patients are awakened from anesthesia to identify the target brain structure.
source: Microelectrode recordings are performed routinely after patients are awakened from anesthesia, to allow electrophysiologists and neurosurgeons to identify the target brain structure along the planned trajectory (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes standard clinical procedure during DBS surgery.

claim: A vibrotactile stimulator was attached to the palm of the hand contralateral to the microelectrode recordings.
source: During this procedure, we attached a vibrotactile stimulator to the palm of the hand contralateral to the microelectrode recordings and estimated the stimulus intensity corresponding to participants' individual tactile detection threshold.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: The main experiment comprised one or two sessions of 71 trials, totaling 48 sessions.
source: Once stable neuronal activity could be recorded in the target brain region (STN or thalamus), we proceeded to the main experiment, which comprised one or two sessions of 71 trials (total: 48 sessions).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and data collection.

claim: Each trial started with an audio 'go' cue, followed by a vibrotactile stimulus applied between 0.5 and 2.5 s after the cue.
source: Each trial started with an audio 'go' cue, followed by a vibrotactile stimulus applied at any time between 0.5 and 2.5 s after the end of the cue (i.e. stimulation window), except for 20% of catch trials in which no stimulus was applied (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the trial structure of the experimental task.

claim: 20% of trials were catch trials in which no stimulus was applied.
source: Each trial started with an audio 'go' cue, followed by a vibrotactile stimulus applied at any time between 0.5 and 2.5 s after the end of the cue (i.e. stimulation window), except for 20% of catch trials in which no stimulus was applied (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design including control trials.

claim: After a random delay of 0.5 to 1 s, a 'respond' cue prompted participants to verbally report whether they felt a vibration.
source: After a random delay ranging from 0.5 to 1 s, a 'respond' cue was played, prompting participants to verbally report whether they felt a vibration or not.
evidence: This describes the response collection procedure.

claim: None of the reported analyses are confounded by motor responses.
source: Therefore, none of the reported analyses are confounded by motor responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the delayed response design of the task.

claim: A staircase procedure kept the stimulus intensity around the detection threshold over the whole experiment.
source: Using a staircase procedure, the stimulus intensity was kept around the detection threshold over the whole experiment.
evidence: This describes the adaptive method used to maintain threshold-level stimulation.

claim: 36 sessions out of 48 were kept for analysis based on objective criteria ensuring hits and misses occurred in commensurate proportions.
source: Based on objective criteria, we excluded a specific series of trials from analyses and focused on trials where hits and misses occurred in commensurate proportions (see Methods). This procedure led us to keep 36 sessions out of 48 with a mean of 24.0 [95% confidence interval = 22.0, 25.9] hit trials and 22.7 [20.8, 24.5] miss trials.
evidence: This describes the data quality control and analysis approach.

claim: Detected and missed stimuli were of similar intensity in most sessions, except in 5 sessions where detected stimuli had higher intensity.
source: Permutation tests at the single-participant level indicated that detected and missed stimuli were of similar intensity, except in 5 sessions for which the intensity of detected stimuli was higher on average.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from permutation tests on the behavioral data.

claim: Detected and missed stimuli had similar onsets in most sessions, with exceptions in 3 sessions.
source: Likewise, detected and missed stimuli had similar onsets, except in 1 session for which stimuli with late onsets were predominantly missed, and in 2 sessions for which stimuli with early onsets were predominantly missed.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from permutation tests on the behavioral data.

claim: The hit rate was comparable between participants with Parkinson's disease (0.51) and essential tremor (0.52).
source: The hit rate was comparable between participants with Parkinson's disease (0.51 [0.49, 0.53]) and essential tremor (0.52 [0.51, 0.53], Wilcoxon rank sum test: W=114.5, p=0.45; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of behavioral performance between patient groups.

claim: The false alarm rate was equivalent between participants with Parkinson's disease (0.24) and essential tremor (0.24).
source: Catch trials were separated into 9.1 [8.1 10.1] correct rejections and 2.1 [1.7, 2.6] false alarms, with an equivalent false alarm rate between participants with Parkinson's disease (0.24 [0.19, 0.28]) and essential tremor (0.24 [0.18, 0.30], Wilcoxon rank sum test: W=145, p=0.76).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of false alarm rates between patient groups.

claim: Intraoperative behavior was similar to behavior during the training session and to behavior in healthy participants using the same task.
source: Intraoperative behavior was similar to the behavior observed during the training session (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and similar to what we found recently in a cohort of healthy participants using the same task (Pereira et al., 2021).
evidence: This comparison is based on data from the current study and a cited previous study.

claim: 48 successful microelectrode recording sessions were performed during 36 surgeries (25 in STN, 23 in thalamus).
source: We performed a total of 48 (STN: 25, Thal: 23) successful microelectrode recording sessions during 36 surgeries for deep brain stimulation electrode implantation.
evidence: This describes the total number of recording sessions obtained.

claim: All neurons showed stable spike amplitudes during the recording.
source: We ensured that all neurons showed stable spike amplitudes during the recording (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: This is a quality control measure verified for all recorded neurons.

claim: 18% of neurons (8/44) were cue-selective, modulating their firing rate during the 500 ms delay following the 'go' cue.
source: There were 8/44 (18 %) cue-selective neurons (Figure 2A; 6 neurons were removed from the analysis due to an insufficient number of trials).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neuronal data analysis.

claim: The number of cue-selective neurons could not have been obtained by chance (p<0.001).
source: We confirmed that these 8 cue-selective neurons could not have been obtained by chance by comparing this number to a null distribution obtained by permuting the sign of the trial-wise differences 1000 times (sign permutation test: p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical test result confirming the significance of the finding.

claim: The proportion of cue-selective neurons was not significantly different in the STN (21%) and thalamus (15%).
source: The proportion of cue-selective neurons was not significantly different in the STN (21%) and thalamus (15%; difference: p=0.31, sign permutation test), and 6 out of 8 neurons showed a decrease in firing rate compared to the pre-cue baseline.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between brain regions.

claim: 6 out of 8 cue-selective neurons showed a decrease in firing rate compared to the pre-cue baseline.
source: The proportion of cue-selective neurons was not significantly different in the STN (21%) and thalamus (15%; difference: p=0.31, sign permutation test), and 6 out of 8 neurons showed a decrease in firing rate compared to the pre-cue baseline.
evidence: This describes the direction of modulation in cue-selective neurons.

claim: 20% of neurons (9/44) were task-selective, showing modulation during the 2 s stimulation window compared to baseline.
source: Next, we investigated how many neurons showed task-selective modulations by comparing firing rates during the 2 s stimulation window to the 500 ms pre-cue baseline, indicating a modulation of their firing rate when a stimulus is expected. There were 9/44 (20%) task-selective neurons (sign permutation test: p=0.003) with a similar proportion in the STN (21%) and thalamus (20%; Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neuronal data analysis.

claim: 8 out of 9 task-selective neurons decreased their firing rate relative to the pre-cue baseline.
source: Interestingly, 8 out of 9 neurons decreased their firing rate relative to the pre-cue baseline.
evidence: This describes the direction of modulation in task-selective neurons.

claim: 44% of task-selective neurons were also cue-selective.
source: In both regions, a significant proportion (44%; permutation test: p<0.001) of the task-selective neurons were also cue-selective, modulating their firing rate before any sensory stimulation necessary for a decision occurred.
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the overlap between neuron types.

claim: Cue- and task-selective neurons are unlikely to be involved in decision-related action selection or cancellation.
source: Therefore, these cue- and task-selective neurons are unlikely to be involved in decision-related action selection or cancellation (Bastin et al., 2014; Mosher et al., 2021) but should be involved in the detection task per se.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of neuronal modulation and cited literature.

claim: 22% of neurons (8/37) were stimulus-selective, modulating their firing rate after stimulus onset.
source: We found 8/37 such stimulus-selective neurons (22%, sign permutation test: p=0.011; Figure 3A–D; 13 neurons were removed due to an insufficient number of trials), with 29% in the STN and 15% in the thalamus.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neuronal data analysis.

claim: Stimulus-selective differences occurred 211 ms ± 34 after the stimulus onset and lasted for an average of 126 ms ± 28.
source: These differences occurred 211 ms±34 after the stimulus onset, lasted for an average of 126 ms±28, and 6 out of 8 neurons showed a decrease in firing rate after the stimulus onset.
evidence: This describes the timing characteristics of stimulus-selective responses.

claim: 6 out of 8 stimulus-selective neurons showed a decrease in firing rate after the stimulus onset.
source: These differences occurred 211 ms±34 after the stimulus onset, lasted for an average of 126 ms±28, and 6 out of 8 neurons showed a decrease in firing rate after the stimulus onset.
evidence: This describes the direction of modulation in stimulus-selective neurons.

claim: Subthalamic and thalamic neurons are modulated by stimulus onset, irrespective of whether it was reported or not.
source: These results show that subthalamic and thalamic neurons are modulated by stimulus onset, irrespective of whether it was reported or not, even though no immediate motor response was required.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stimulus-selective neuron data.

claim: 8 neurons (23%) showed a significant difference in firing rate between hits and misses after stimulus onset.
source: Of the 50 neurons recorded, 35 were associated with periods of high-quality behavior, allowing us to assume tactile stimulation at the perceptual threshold. We found 8 neurons (23%) showing a significant difference between hits and misses after stimulus onset (trial permutation test: p=0.0060; Figure 4A–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is the main quantitative finding regarding perception-selective neurons.

claim: Each perception-selective neuron was found in a different participant.
source: Each neuron was found in a different participant.
evidence: This describes the distribution of perception-selective neurons across participants.

claim: The proportion of perception-selective neurons was similar in the STN (27%) and the thalamus (20%).
source: The proportion of these perception-selective neurons was similar in the STN (27%) and the thalamus (20%; difference: p=0.529; trial permutation test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between brain regions.

claim: Differences in firing rates for perception-selective neurons occurred on average 160 ms ± 36 after stimulus onset and lasted for 100 ms ± 10.
source: These differences in firing rates occurred on average 160 ms±36 after the stimulus onset and lasted for an average of 100 ms±10.
evidence: This describes the timing characteristics of perception-selective responses.

claim: The timings of sensory and perception effects showed a bimodal distribution with an early cluster (149 ms for sensory, 121 ms for perception) and a late cluster (330 ms for sensory, 315 ms for perception).
source: We note that the timings of sensory and perception effects in Figures 3 and 4 showed a bimodal distribution with an early cluster (149 ms for sensory neurons; 121 ms for perception neurons; c.f. Methods) and a late cluster (330 ms for sensory neurons; 315 ms for perception neurons; Figure 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the timing distribution of neural effects.

claim: 6 out of 8 perception-selective neurons had higher firing rates for missed trials than hit trials.
source: We note that 6 out of 8 neurons had higher firing rates for missed trials than hit trials.
evidence: This describes the direction of modulation in perception-selective neurons.

claim: None of the perception-selective neurons showed sustained differences between the highest and lowest stimulus amplitudes.
source: None of the aforementioned neurons showed sustained differences between the highest and lowest stimulus amplitudes nor between early and late stimulus onset within the 2 s stimulus window (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a control analysis ruling out confounding factors.

claim: None of the perception-selective neurons showed sustained differences between early and late stimulus onset.
source: None of the aforementioned neurons showed sustained differences between the highest and lowest stimulus amplitudes nor between early and late stimulus onset within the 2 s stimulus window (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a control analysis ruling out confounding factors.

claim: There was little overlap between task-, stimulus-, and perception-selective neurons.
source: Qualitatively, we found little overlap between task-, stimulus-, and perception-selective neurons (one neuron selective for all three categories, one task- and perception-selective neuron, two stimulus- and perception-selective neurons, and one task- and perception-selective neuron; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes the functional diversity of neurons in the recorded regions.

claim: The two subcortical structures display neurons with several different functional roles.
source: This result suggests that these two subcortical structures display neurons with several different functional roles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed diversity of neuron selectivity types.

claim: No clear indication was found that neurons with a beta-band oscillatory component were more or less selective.
source: We also found no clear indication that neurons with a beta-band oscillatory component were more or less selective.
evidence: This is a negative finding from analysis of oscillatory properties.

claim: The findings that neurons in the thalamus modulate their activity according to tactile detection add to existing evidence for the role of the thalamus in perceptual consciousness.
source: Our findings that neurons in the thalamus modulate their activity according to tactile detection add to the existing evidence in favor of the role of the thalamus for perceptual consciousness.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of existing literature.

claim: Thalamic activity and thalamocortical loops are often considered key to gate sensory stimuli to conscious access.
source: Indeed, thalamic activity and, more precisely, thalamocortical loops are often considered key to gate sensory stimuli to conscious access (Ward, 2013).
evidence: This is established theory cited from the literature.

claim: In nonhuman primates, oscillatory thalamic activity predicts tactile detection.
source: In nonhuman primates, for example, oscillatory thalamic activity predicts tactile detection (Haegens et al., 2014), and functional interactions between the somatosensory thalamus and the cortex increase when a tactile stimulus is detected (Tauste Campo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited evidence from animal studies.

claim: Functional interactions between the somatosensory thalamus and the cortex increase when a tactile stimulus is detected in nonhuman primates.
source: In nonhuman primates, for example, oscillatory thalamic activity predicts tactile detection (Haegens et al., 2014), and functional interactions between the somatosensory thalamus and the cortex increase when a tactile stimulus is detected (Tauste Campo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited evidence from animal studies.

claim: In humans, thalamic local field potentials and fMRI activity were higher for seen vs unseen stimuli.
source: In humans, thalamic local field potentials and fMRI activity were higher for seen vs unseen stimuli (Kronemer et al., 2022; Levinson et al., 2021), and causal effects of thalamic stimulation on the levels of consciousness have been found (Schiff et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited evidence from human studies.

claim: Causal effects of thalamic stimulation on the levels of consciousness have been found in humans.
source: In humans, thalamic local field potentials and fMRI activity were higher for seen vs unseen stimuli (Kronemer et al., 2022; Levinson et al., 2021), and causal effects of thalamic stimulation on the levels of consciousness have been found (Schiff et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited evidence from human studies.

claim: Perception-selective neurons in the STN may determine stimulus detection through the regulation of decisional processes.
source: Concerning the STN, a possibility is that perception-selective neurons determine stimulus detection through the regulation of decisional processes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the STN findings.

claim: Previous studies reported a modulatory role of subthalamic activity on decisional processes by elevating the decisional threshold on accumulated sensory evidence.
source: Indeed, previous studies reported a modulatory role of subthalamic activity on decisional processes, notably by elevating the decisional threshold on accumulated sensory evidence (Bogacz and Gurney, 2007; Cavanagh et al., 2011; Green et al., 2013; Herz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited evidence from previous research on STN function.

claim: Evidence accumulation is at play during conscious detection in cortical neurons.
source: In a recent study in which we measured the activity of cortical neurons in a similar task, we showed that evidence accumulation is also at play during conscious detection (Pereira et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited evidence from the authors' previous work.

claim: Percepts fade in and out of consciousness when evidence accumulated by cortical neurons passes a given threshold.
source: Based on this finding, we proposed that percepts fade in and out of consciousness when evidence accumulated by cortical neurons passes a given threshold (Pereira et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal from the authors' previous work.

claim: The contribution of subthalamic neurons to decisional processes may also regulate the threshold at which accumulated evidence gives rise to a conscious percept.
source: The present results, therefore, indicate that the contribution of subthalamic neurons to decisional processes is not limited to discrimination tasks or motor planning, but may also regulate the threshold at which accumulated evidence gives rise to a conscious percept.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in light of previous work.

claim: The STN has an inhibitory role on the cortex.
source: Considering the inhibitory role of the STN on the cortex (Mink, 1996), the fact that many of the perception-selective neurons we found had higher firing rates for misses than for hits suggests a role in elevating that threshold, similar to what is found in decision tasks manipulating conflict or cautiousness and requiring immediate responses (Bastin et al., 2014; Cavanagh et al., 2011; Frank et al., 2007; Herz et al., 2016; Mosher et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about STN function cited from the literature.

claim: The STN plays an important role in a subcortical network gating conscious access, although it might not encode conscious content per se.
source: Thus, our results suggest that the STN plays an important role in a subcortical network gating conscious access, although it might not encode conscious content per se (Aru et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with reference to theoretical distinctions in consciousness research.

claim: A distinct population of neurons in both the STN and thalamus modulated their firing rate both after the cue and during the task, before the stimulus onset.
source: Apart from perception-selective neurons, we also found a distinct population of neurons in both the STN and thalamus that modulated their firing rate both after the cue and during the task, and therefore much before the stimulus onset.
evidence: This describes an additional finding about neuron types.

claim: Neurons that modulate before stimulus onset could be involved in task switching.
source: These neurons cannot be involved in detection-related processes but could instead be involved in task switching (Hikosaka and Isoda, 2010; Laquitaine et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on cited literature.

claim: Microelectrode recordings could reconcile the multiple roles ascribed to subcortical structures by exposing the variety of functional roles of neurons inside those regions.
source: Microelectrode recordings could therefore reconcile the multiple roles ascribed to subcortical structures by exposing the variety of functional roles of the neurons inside those regions.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the value of the methodological approach.

claim: Neurons were found that modulated their firing rates after the stimulus onset, irrespective of detection, similar to animal works in the STN and thalamus.
source: We also found neurons that modulated their firing rates after the stimulus onset, irrespective of detection, similar to animal works in the STN (Al Tannir et al., 2023; Coizet et al., 2009) and thalamus (Tauste Campo et al., 2019; Vázquez et al., 2012).
evidence: This finding is contextualized with citations to animal studies.

claim: The results should be taken with caution due to the small number of neurons and insufficient trials to test computational mechanisms.
source: Our results should be taken with caution as they are based on a small number of neurons due to the high complexity of intraoperative recordings, and because the number of trials we could collect was not sufficient to test the computational mechanisms underlying the neuronal activity we recorded.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the study's limitations.

claim: Both sensory and perception effects could be grouped into an early and a late cluster.
source: Interestingly, we found that both sensory and perception effects could be grouped into an early and a late cluster.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the timing of neural effects.

claim: The early cluster's average timing around 150 ms post-stimulus corresponds to the onset of the somatosensory awareness negativity.
source: The early cluster's average timing around 150 ms post-stimulus corresponds to the onset of a putative cortical correlate of tactile consciousness, the somatosensory awareness negativity (Dembski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation linking the timing to known EEG markers cited from the literature.

claim: It is unclear whether the somatosensory awareness negativity is related to perceptual consciousness or selective attention.
source: It is unclear, however, whether these markers are related to perceptual consciousness or selective attention (Dembski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of ambiguity in the literature cited.

claim: The late cluster is centered around 300 ms and could correspond to the P3b.
source: The late cluster is centered around 300 ms and could correspond to a well-known electroencephalographic marker, the P3b (Polich, 2007), whose association with perceptual consciousness has been questioned (Dembski et al., 2021; Pitts et al., 2014), although brain activity related to consciousness has been observed at similar timing even in the absence of report demands (Sergent et al., 2021; Stockart et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation linking timing to known EEG markers with citations.

claim: The association of the P3b with perceptual consciousness has been questioned.
source: The late cluster is centered around 300 ms and could correspond to a well-known electroencephalographic marker, the P3b (Polich, 2007), whose association with perceptual consciousness has been questioned (Dembski et al., 2021; Pitts et al., 2014), although brain activity related to consciousness has been observed at similar timing even in the absence of report demands (Sergent et al., 2021; Stockart et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a summary of debate in the literature with citations.

claim: Brain activity related to consciousness has been observed at similar timing (300 ms) even in the absence of report demands.
source: The late cluster is centered around 300 ms and could correspond to a well-known electroencephalographic marker, the P3b (Polich, 2007), whose association with perceptual consciousness has been questioned (Dembski et al., 2021; Pitts et al., 2014), although brain activity related to consciousness has been observed at similar timing even in the absence of report demands (Sergent et al., 2021; Stockart et al., 2024).
evidence: This is cited evidence from no-report paradigm studies.

claim: The timing clusters contain neurons with both increased and decreased firing rates following the stimulus onset.
source: It is also important to note that these clusters contain neurons with both increased and decreased firing rates following the stimulus onset, similar to what was observed previously in the posterior parietal cortex (Pereira et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the heterogeneity of responses and cites a similar finding in cortex.

claim: Future studies should rule out the presence of motor preparation triggered by perceived stimuli.
source: Future studies ruling out the presence of motor preparation triggered by perceived stimuli (Bennur and Gold, 2011; Fang et al., 2024; Twomey et al., 2016) and verifying that similar neuronal activity occurs in the absence of task demands (no-reports; Tsuchiya et al., 2015) or attention (Wyart and Tallon-Baudry, 2008) will be useful to support that subcortical neurons contribute specifically to perceptual consciousness.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research with citations to relevant methodological concerns.

claim: The study provides neurophysiological evidence from single neurons in humans that subcortical structures play a significant role in tactile detection.
source: In sum, our study provides neurophysiological evidence from single neurons in humans that subcortical structures play a significant role in tactile detection either by themselves (Ward, 2013) or through their numerous connections with the cortex (Dehaene and Changeux, 2011).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study with citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: A comprehensive account of the neural correlates of consciousness should not be cortico-centric but also consider subcortical contributions.
source: A comprehensive account of the neural correlates of consciousness should, therefore, not be cortico-centric but also consider subcortical contributions.
evidence: This is the main theoretical implication of the findings.

claim: High-impedance electrophysiological signals were recorded from microelectrodes inserted intraoperatively in the STN of 32 participants with Parkinson's disease or essential tremor.
source: We recorded high-impedance electrophysiological signals from microelectrodes inserted intraoperatively in the STN of 32 participants with Parkinson's disease or essential tremor undergoing deep brain stimulation electrode implantation surgeries (N=36; 4 participants had two surgeries, one for each side; convenience sampling).
evidence: This describes the participant sample and recording method.

claim: For individuals with Parkinson's disease, the age at the time of recording was 60.4 ± 2.7 years.
source: For individuals with Parkinson's disease, the age at the time of the recording was 60.4±2.7 years, and the average UPDRS III score was 40.6±3.0 prior to surgery and was reduced to 20.8±2.8 after the surgery (p=0.0015, z=3.18).
evidence: This is demographic and clinical data for the Parkinson's disease participants.

claim: The average UPDRS III score for Parkinson's disease participants was 40.6 ± 3.0 prior to surgery and was reduced to 20.8 ± 2.8 after surgery.
source: For individuals with Parkinson's disease, the age at the time of the recording was 60.4±2.7 years, and the average UPDRS III score was 40.6±3.0 prior to surgery and was reduced to 20.8±2.8 after the surgery (p=0.0015, z=3.18).
evidence: This is clinical outcome data showing improvement after surgery.

claim: For individuals with essential tremor, the age at the time of recording was 68.9 ± 3.2 years.
source: We also recorded intraoperatively in the thalamus of individuals with essential tremor undergoing deep brain stimulation surgeries. The age at the time of the recording was 68.9±3.2 years, and the average TETRA motor score was 20.1±2.9 prior to surgery.
evidence: This is demographic and clinical data for the essential tremor participants.

claim: The average TETRA motor score for essential tremor participants was 20.1 ± 2.9 prior to surgery.
source: We also recorded intraoperatively in the thalamus of individuals with essential tremor undergoing deep brain stimulation surgeries. The age at the time of the recording was 68.9±3.2 years, and the average TETRA motor score was 20.1±2.9 prior to surgery.
evidence: This is clinical data for the essential tremor participants.

claim: The study was approved by the institutional review board of the West Virginia University Hospital.
source: The study was approved by the institutional review board of the West Virginia University Hospital (WVU02HSC17; #1709745061), and all participants provided written informed consent prior to any data collection.
evidence: This is ethical approval information.

claim: All participants provided written informed consent prior to any data collection.
source: The study was approved by the institutional review board of the West Virginia University Hospital (WVU02HSC17; #1709745061), and all participants provided written informed consent prior to any data collection.
evidence: This is ethical procedure information.

claim: The tactile detection task was programmed in MATLAB using the Psychophysics toolbox.
source: Participants performed a tactile detection task programmed in MATLAB using the Psychophysics toolbox (Brainard, 1997; Kleiner et al., 2007; Pelli, 1997).
evidence: This describes the software used for the experimental task.

claim: 18 out of 36 surgeries included participants who were trained a few days before the surgery.
source: When possible, participants were trained a few days before the surgery (N=18/36 surgeries).
evidence: This describes the training procedure for a subset of participants.

claim: Stimuli were applied using an MMC3 Haptuator vibrotactile device from TactileLabs Inc driven by a 230 Hz sinusoid audio signal.
source: Stimuli were applied using an MMC3 Haptuator vibrotactile device from TactileLabs Inc (Montréal, Canada) driven by a 230 Hz sinusoid audio signal.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the stimulation device.

claim: A 1-up/1-down adaptive staircase procedure ensured that the intensity was kept around the perceptual threshold.
source: During the main task, a 1-up/1-down adaptive staircase procedure (Levitt, 1971) ensured that the intensity was kept around the perceptual threshold by increasing the intensity by 5% after a miss trial and decreasing the intensity by 5% after a hit trial.
evidence: This describes the adaptive procedure with a citation to the method.

claim: The absolute stimulus intensity is not informative and cannot be compared across patients and sessions.
source: Of note, the absolute stimulus intensity is not informative and cannot be compared across patients and sessions, as it varied according to different factors (e.g. the length of the cable or the manner with which the tactile stimulator was strapped onto the palm).
evidence: This is a methodological note about the limitations of the intensity measurements.

claim: STN or thalamus targets and trajectories were defined preoperatively using CranialSuite based on MRI scans.
source: STN or thalamus targets and trajectories were defined preoperatively using CranialSuite (Neurotargeting Inc, Nashville, TN, USA) based on MRI scans.
evidence: This describes the surgical planning procedure.

claim: Electrophysiological data were recorded from the 5 mm tip of the microelectrode, referenced to the guide cannula.
source: Electrophysiological data were recorded from the 5 mm tip of the microelectrode, referenced to the guide cannula, and an adaptive line noise canceller was applied.
evidence: This describes the recording configuration.

claim: Data were digitized using either a Guideline 4000 LP+ amplifier at 30 kHz (N=21 surgeries) or a Guideline 5 amplifier at 32 kHz and resampled offline to 30 kHz (N=14 surgeries).
source: Data were digitized either using a Guideline 4000 LP+ amplifier (FHC, ME, USA) at 30 kHz (N=21 surgeries) or using a Guideline 5 amplifier (FHC, ME, USA) at 32 kHz and resampled offline to 30 kHz (N=14 surgeries).
evidence: This describes the data acquisition systems used.

claim: For 34 out of 50 neurons, preoperative MRI and postoperative CT scans were available to precisely reconstruct surgical trajectories and recording locations.
source: For 34/50 neurons, preoperative MRI and postoperative CT scans (co-registered in patient's native space using CranialSuite) were available to precisely reconstruct surgical trajectories and recording locations (for the remaining 16 neurons, localizations were based on neurosurgical planning and confirmed by electrophysiological recordings at various depths).
evidence: This describes the anatomical localization method for most neurons.

claim: Recording depths were projected onto an MNI-coordinate space and compared against the Ilinsky atlas.
source: Recording depths were inspected along the trajectories in patient's native space, projected onto an MNI-coordinate space and compared against the Ilinsky atlas (Ilinsky et al., 2018), which delineates distinct thalamic sub-territories based on a marker of γ-aminobutyric acid on sections of postmortem human brains.
evidence: This describes the anatomical localization procedure with citation to the atlas used.

claim: R 4.1.2 and the tidyverse package were used to analyze behavioral data.
source: We used R 4.1.2 (R Development Core Team, 2013) and the tidyverse (Wickham et al., 2019) package to analyze behavioral data.
evidence: This describes the software used for behavioral analysis.

claim: Neuronal spikes were detected and clustered using an online semiautomatic spike sorting algorithm (Osort).
source: Neuronal spikes were detected and clustered using an online semiautomatic spike sorting algorithm (Osort) (Rutishauser et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes the spike sorting method with citation.

claim: Instantaneous firing rates were estimated using a sliding Gaussian kernel with a standard deviation of 40 ms and 1 ms steps.
source: We estimated instantaneous firing rates using a sliding Gaussian kernel with a standard deviation of 40 ms and 1 ms steps.
evidence: This describes the method for computing firing rates.

claim: The standard error of the mean for average firing rates over time was estimated using a bootstrap procedure with 1000 resamplings.
source: When displaying the resulting average firing rates over time, we estimated the standard error of the mean using a bootstrap procedure with 1000 resamplings.
evidence: This describes the statistical method for error estimation.

claim: Permutation tests were used instead of binomial tests to test whether a reported number of neurons could have been obtained by chance.
source: We used permutation tests instead of binomial tests to test whether a reported number of neurons could have been obtained by chance.
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used.

claim: A putative neuron was considered sensory-selective when the length of a cluster was above 80 ms, corresponding to twice the standard deviation of the smoothing kernel.
source: A putative neuron was considered sensory-selective when the length of a cluster was above 80 ms, corresponding to twice the standard deviation of the smoothing kernel used to compute the firing rate.
evidence: This describes the criterion for classifying sensory-selective neurons.

claim: A two-component Gaussian mixture distribution was fitted to measure bimodal timings of effect latencies.
source: To measure bimodal timings of effect latencies, we fitted a two-component Gaussian mixture distribution to the data in Figure 5 by minimizing the mean square error with an interior-point method.
evidence: This describes the statistical method for analyzing timing distributions.
